Ed. 2026, 65, e22940 doi.org/10.1002/anie.202522940 Batteries Very Important Paper Modulating Li+ and Polysulfide Solvation with Low-Density Moderately Solvating Electrolytes for Lithium–Sulfur Batteries Tianxing Lai, Kameron Liao, and Arumugam Manthiram* Abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries show great promise as the next-generation rechargeable batteries, yet they still suffer from polysulfide shuttling and interphasial instability.
Electrolyte, as the medium for ion transport and sulfur conversion, plays a crucial role in overcoming these challenges.

Here, we introduce a moderately solvating electrolyte (MSE) based on low-density, low-viscosity, and nonfluorinated ether co-solvents that balances polysulfide suppression, Li metal stabilization, and redox kinetics.

Through multiple solvent–solvent and solvent-ion interactions, the optimized MSE weakens Li+-solvent pairing while strengthening cation–anion interactions, thereby lowering the desolvation barrier and promoting the formation of a favorable solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI).

Meanwhile, MSE limits the polysulfide dissolution but improves the accessibility of active material through better wettability and tailored solvation environment, leading to an altered sulfur deposition mechanism with β – α conversion.

This approach enables a stable cycling of highmass loading Li–S cells (> 3.5 mg cm−2) at both room temperature and 45 °C (where shuttling and side reactions are severer), and demonstrates a pouch cell with lean electrolyte content (4.5 μL mg s−1).
This work highlights a practical route to develop high-performance electrolyte for Li–S cells and provides mechanistic insights into their operation.

Introduction Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries have attracted intense interest as a next-generation energy-storage technology because they combine high theoretical energy density (2600 W h kg−1) with low material cost and less supply chain issues (compared to current transition-metal based chemistries).[1] Li–S batteries are particularly attractive for weight and costsensitive applications, such as electric vehicles, aviation, and space equipment.
However, practical deployment of Li–S cells is impeded by several interconnected challenges.
During cycling, sulfur undergoes multistep redox reactions that form electrolyte soluble lithium polysulfide (LiPS) intermediates.
They lead to an infamous phenomenon called shuttling, which then causes active material loss and continuous parasitic reactions at the lithium–metal anode.

Meanwhile, the lithium anode suffers from intrinsically poor interphasial stability, while the sulfur cathode is limited by its low conductivity, poor redox kinetics, and large volume changes during cycling.

These issues could be even more challenging when practical conditions like high sulfur loading and lean electrolyte are employed, leading to poor energy density and cycle life.[2,3] To address these obstacles, extensive efforts have been made in the field.

Cathode engineering, including ingeniously designed carbon hosts and catalyst materials, has proven effective in ameliorating sulfur conversion kinetics and mitigating LiPS shuttling.[4–11] Nevertheless, electrolyte, as the solvation and transport medium for Li+ ion and polysulfide, plays a decisive role in regulating polysulfide chemistry and interphasial stability of both electrodes.
In fact, electrolyte design offers a feasible and arguably more scalable route to remedy the unique polysulfide-related problems in Li–S cells.

A range of electrolyte strategies has, therefore, been explored, including solvent and salt selection, concentration tuning, targeted additives.[12–17] The etherbased 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) / 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) electrolyte remains the benchmark in the field because it offers reasonable sulfur conversion kinetics and compatibility with Li anode; however, it provides limited control over LiPS shuttling.
Carbonate electrolytes are widely employed in commercial Li-ion batteries.

They are normally considered incompatible with Li–S chemistry due to the nucleophilic attack by LiPSs, but they could be an option as they can limit the LiPS dissolution by forming a protective cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) layer.[18–20] However, the use of carbonate electrolytes in Li–S cells requires extreme confinement of sulfur at the cathode, such as covalently bonded or sophisticated structures.[21–23] Moreover, carbonate electrolytes show inferior compatibility with Li metal, limiting the long-term cyclability of the anode.

However, the standard of choosing such co-solvent and a detailed understanding of how it influences the polysulfide solvating environment are still lacking.
Here, we present new MSE designs employing a series of low-density, lowviscosity, low-cost, and nonfluorinated ether co-solvents.
Their influence on the Li+ ion and polysulfide solvations are systematically investigated.
It is revealed that MSEs modulate the solvating environment for not only Li+ ions, but also salt and polysulfide anions, through multiple intermolecular interactions.

As a result, the desolvation barrier for Li+ ion is reduced and an inorganic-enriched solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) is formed on the anode surface, leading to a better reversibility of Li plating and stripping (Figure 1a).
Meanwhile, the polysulfide behavior in the electrolyte is altered, mitigating shuttling and reducing active material loss.
Operando and electrochemical characterizations further reveal the change in sulfur conversion pathway and redox kinetics with MSE.
Finally, the optimized MSE enables high sulfur utilization and stable cycling of Li || S cells with practical S loadings and limited electrolyte conditions at both room temperature and 45 °C.
The effectiveness of this electrolyte at larger scale is also demonstrated with pouch cells.

Results and Discussion Based on their structural and physicochemical properties, a series of single-oxygen ethers, including methyl tert–butyl ether (MtBE), cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME), sec-butyl methyl ether (SBME), and tert-amyl methyl ether (TAME), were selected as the solvents to regulate the solvating ability of the conventional DOL/DME electrolyte (Figure 1b and Table S1).
These solvents feature only one solvating O atom and possess sufficient steric hindrance that limits their solvating capability for Li+.

Unlike nonsolvating diluents, such as highly fluorinated ethers, these solvents show some degree of solvating power, but still have much lower solubility for LiPS compared to DME and DOL, which can lead to unique local solvating environment (Figure 1c and Figure S2).
Meanwhile, they feature slight structural differences among each other that help fine tune the solvation structures and better understand their effect in the electrolyte.
The designed MSEs with 30 vol% of these solvents are labeled as MSE-MtBE, MSE-CPME, MSE-SBME, and MSE-TAME, respectively (detailed compositions given in the Supporting Information).
Owing to the low density of these solvents, these MSEs exhibit lower densities (e.g., 1.04 g cm−3 for MSE-MtBE) compared to DOL/DME baseline (1.16 g cm−3).

Research Article Density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm that DME, due to its bidentate solvation, has a strong binding energy of 0.643 eV to a Li+ ion (Figure 1d,e).
In contrast, three of the four selected solvents bind significantly weaker with binding energy values of ∼0.15 eV.
Note that CPME shows a binding energy of ∼0.325 eV, which is even slightly higher than that of DOL.
This indicates that the five-member ring structure at one side of the O atom limits the steric hindrance compared to other solvents.
Lithium-Ion Solvation and Anode Stabilization The solvation structures of MSEs were examined with Raman spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.

Raman spectra display a blue shift of the S─N─S vibrational mode of TFSI for all the MSEs (742.5– 743.1 cm−1) compared to the DOL/DME baseline (741.6 cm−1), suggesting more contact-ion pairs (CIPs) and salt aggregates (AGGs) formed in MSEs (Figure S3).
This is also demonstrated by the peak deconvolution results, which show a clear increase in the intensity of the CIP/AGG peak at ∼745 cm−1 for MSEs.
NMR spectroscopy was employed to provide a more precise understanding of the solvation structures.
In the 7Li NMR spectra, all the peaks in MSEs show a downfield shift from −1.19 ppm in the DOL/DME baseline electrolyte, indicating less electron shielding around the Li+ ion (Figure 2a).
This involves the combination of two competing effectsshielding from the increase of cation–anion pairing and de-shielding from the reduction of Li+–solvent interactions.

Since DME is a strong solvating solvent and the electrons on its O atoms strongly shield Li+, replacing it with an anion or a weakly solvating solvent in the solvation shell usually results in more de-shielding.[35–37] Note that Raman results show a similar increase of cation-anion pairing in all MSEs.

Therefore, the fact that the 7Li peak shifts to greater downfield in MSE-MtBE and MSE-SBME indicates their stronger ability to pull DME and DOL away from the Li+ ion, as well as their weaker interactions with Li+ ion, compared to other MSEs.

Similarly, in the 19F spectra, the TFSI−anion peaks shift upfield in MSEs compared to the DOL/DME electrolyte (−80.17 ppm) due to stronger Li+–anion pairing and weaker anion-solvent interactions (Figure S4).
Nevertheless, unlike the 7Li peak, the upfield shift of the 19F peak in MSE- MtBE is the smallest among MSEs, indicating potentially stronger interactions between its protons and TFSI−anions.

This is further demonstrated with the 2D 19F diffusion ordered spectroscopy (DOSY) NMR spectra, where TFSI−anion exhibits a slightly smaller diffusion coefficient of 4.37 × 10−10 m2 s−1 in MSE-MtBE compared to 5.01 × 10−10 m2 s−1 in DOL/DME (Figure S5). 1H NMR results provide further insight into these solventrelated interactions.
After adding MtBE into the DOL/DME mixture, the 1H peaks for DOL and DME shift downfield owing to the MtBE-induced solvent-solvent interactions (Figure 2b).
The O atoms in MtBE pull electrons away from the H atoms in DOL and DME, resulting in less electron shielding of the H atoms.
When Li salt is introduced into the system, DME pairs more with the Li+ ions, reducing its interactions with other solvents.
The MtBE peaks show an upfield shift due to this effect, as well as the solvent-anion interactions discussed earlier.

Moreover, by comparing 1H NMR spectra for all the MSEs with salt, the 1H peaks for DME and DOL in MSE-MtBE show the most downfield shift, suggesting the strongest capability of MtBE to reduce electron density on DME and DOL (Figure 2c).
This could be one of the reasons why DME and DOL show weaker interactions with Li+ ion in MSE-MtBE compared to other MSEs.
These solvation properties and interactions were further demonstrated with molecular dynamics (MD) and DFT calculations.

As shown in the MD results, the coordination number (CN) of ODME around Li+ in the first solvation shell (∼2–4 Å) decreases in MSEs compared to DOL/DME, with MtBE having the lowest coordination number (Figures 2d and S6).
This confirms that all the MSEs can weaken the coordination between Li+ and DME, but MtBE does so more effectively, aligning well with the NMR results.
Meanwhile, radial distribution function (RDF) peaks of the O atom on MSEs in the first solvation sheath can be observed, demonstrating their limited, yet not negligible, solvating power (Figure S7).
DFT calculations of DME– solvent complexes reveal that DME–MtBE has the highest binding energy of 0.189 eV among all MSEs, confirming their strongest intermolecular interactions (Figure 2e).

Furthermore, small-angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) was performed to probe the inhomogeneities, clustering, and intermolecular spacing in the electrolytes across microscopic to mesoscopic scales.[38] Taking MtBE-MSE as an example, both MtBE-MSE and DOL/DME baseline display a broad peak in their SAXS curves at a high scattering factor (q) value (> 1 Å−1), corresponding to the average molecule size or intermolecular distances (Figure S8).
Meanwhile, there is also a shoulder peak at ∼0.6 Å−1, which is related to the CIP/AGG formed in the electrolyte (with a size of ∼10 Å).
The fact that MtBE-MSE shows higher intensity in this region confirms the formation of more CIPs and AGGs in the electrolyte.

In addition, MtBE-MSE exhibits higher intensity in the q range of 0.05–0.4 Å−1, suggesting more pronounced clustering at a larger scale (∼10 s of nm), potentially owing to the introduced solvent-solvent interactions with MtBE.
The altered solvation properties of MSEs play an important role in influencing the reaction kinetics at the Li-metal side, which is examined with electrochemical tests.
Tafel plots of Li || Li symmetric cells were derived from linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) scans (Figure S9).
By fitting these Tafel plots, the exchange current density of the redox reaction can be obtained.
MSEs exhibit higher exchange current densities compared to DOL/DME, indicating faster electrochemical reaction kinetics on Li metal.
Temperaturedependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on fresh Li || Li cells provides more insight into the Li+ transport kinetics at the interphase.

Through the distribution of relaxation time (DRT) analysis for the EIS data, there is one major peak within the time constant range of 10−4 to 10−2, corresponding to the semicircle at mid-frequency region in the Nyquist plots (Figures S10 and S11).

MSEs show significantly lower Rct compared to DOL/DME, resulting from the weakened Li+-solvent interactions discussed before.
This leads to easier desolvation and explains faster redox kinetics at the Li metal anode.

Nevertheless, after fitting these temperature-dependent Rct based on the Arrhenius equation to obtain the activation energy, MSEs and the baseline exhibit relatively similar activation barrier for the desolvation process (Figure 2f).

This suggests that, even in MSEs, the main energy barrier for desolvation is still coming from the dissociation of the Li+-DME pairing, while the factors like total number of strongly bound DME affects the pre-exponential factor in the Arrhenius equation and the overall Rct.

Note that MtBE indeed presents the smallest activation energy, proving its effectiveness in reducing not only the quantity, but also the strength of Li+-DME pairing through solvent-solvent interactions.
Next, Li || Ni cells were assembled to investigate the reversibility of Li-metal plating and stripping.
By utilizing the Aurbach method, coulombic efficiencies (CE) of Li plating and stripping were obtained for each electrolyte.
MSE- MtBE achieves the highest CE of 99.5% among all MSEs, whereas the DOL/DME electrolyte only realizes a CE of 98.0% (Figures 2g and S12).
Long-term cyclabilities of Limetal in Li || Li symmetric cells were further evaluated for MSE-MtBE and the baseline.

As shown in Figure 2h, the cell with MSE-MtBE demonstrates slightly lower plating and stripping overpotential and stable cycling for over 600 h at a current density of 1 mA cm−2, whereas the DOL/DME cell failed after 400 h.
These results showcase the ability of MSE-MtBE to stabilize the Li deposition.

Research Article MSE-MtBE provides an optimal balance of cation-anion, anion-solvent, and solvent–solvent interactions.
It weakens excessive Li+-solvent binding and promotes favorable cationanion contacts, leading to reduced desolvation barrier and superior anode performance.
Further insights into how MSEs influence polysulfide solvation and cathode performance will be discussed in the next section.
Polysulfide Solvation and Conversion Kinetics LiPSs play a pivotal role in affecting the redox reaction kinetics in Li–S batteries.
Although MSEs possess lower LiPS solubility than the DOL/DME baseline, they still involve a soluble LiPS-mediated redox pathway (Figure S13).
Therefore, investigating LiPS behavior in the electrolyte is crucial for understanding the cathode kinetics and overall cell performance.
NMR tests were first conducted on 0.1 M Li2S6 solutions (without other salts) to evaluate the solvating environment of LiPS.
In the 7Li spectra, the peak downshifts from 0.17 ppm in DOL/DME to 0.28 ppm in MtBE (Figure 3a).
Other MSEs also show a downfield shift (except CPME), but less pronounced compared to MtBE.
This could mainly result from reduced Li+-solvent interactions with more Li+ and S62− pairing, similar to the case of regular electrolytes discussed in the previous section.
Furthermore, 1H and 7Li DOSY NMR studies were employed to probe the diffusivity of the solvent and Li+ ion in the Li2S6 solution (Figure 3b,c).

Interestingly, in the solution with MtBE, DME and Li+ show diffusion coefficients of 1.91 × 10−9 and 5.62 × 10−10 m2 s−1, respectively, which are higher compared to 1.26 × 10−9 and 4.47 × 10−10 m2 s−1, respectively, in the DOL/DME solution.

These higher diffusivities with the addition of MtBE likely arise from the overall reduced solvent-Li+ binding, as well as the low viscosity of MtBE, which promotes faster mass transport in the actual cells for MSEs.
Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations provide further insights into the solvating environment with polysulfide in the electrolyte.
In the DOL/DME system, Li+ is predominantly solvated by DME and DOL molecules, making the S62−anion to dissociate from Li+ (Figures 3d and S14).
In contrast, RDF and representative AIMD snapshots for the MtBE-containing formulation show an increased propensity for Li+–S62−pairing (Figures 3e,f and S14).
Moreover, MtBE tends to pull DME away from Li+, reducing the number of DME molecules in the inner solvation shell of the Li+ and S62−complex.

These results indicate that MSE-MtBE most effectively shifts polysulfide solvation toward more ion pairing, which could directly affect polysulfide migration and conversion; accordingly, MSE-MtBE was selected for further evaluation.

Due to the reduction of LiPS solubility and regulation of solvation structures, the LiPS shuttling effect is expected to be effectively mitigated in MSE-MtBE, which could make a substantial impact on the cyclability of Li–S cells.
To validate this, a shuttling current test was performed on Li || S cells by holding the voltage at 2.25 V during discharge, the point when high-order LiPS largely formed.
As shown in Figure S15, the current in the DOL/DME cell quickly changes direction and levels off at ∼0.047 mA, indicating obvious LiPS shuttling.
In contrast, the MSE-MtBE cell shows much slower current change, and the shuttle current stabilizes at ∼0.013 mA, demonstrating its ability to suppress shuttling.
Several more tests were conducted to better assess the impact of electrolyte on sulfur conversion kinetics.

Pairing the galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) with EIS is an effective approach to study cell polarization.[40] By applying this GITT-EIS method to Li || S cells with practical sulfur loading, the overall cell polarization (ηtotal) can be resolved into three contributions: ohmic (ηohm), activation (ηact), and concentration (ηconc) polarizations. ηohm captures ionic resistance in the bulk electrolyte as well as electronic and contact resistances within the electrodes and cell hardware; it can be extracted from the high-frequency intercept on the Nyquist plot. ηact corresponds to the energy barrier of the interfacial charge-transfer process and, together with ηohm, produces the instantaneous voltage jump observed whenever the current is stepped during GITT measurement.

Finally, ηconc arises from mass-transport limitations when Li+ ions and LiPSs are locally depleted at the electrode surface due to electrochemical reactions; ηconc can be obtained from the gradual voltage drift toward equilibrium potential during the relaxation period in GITT.

For both the cell with MSE-MtBE and DOL/DME electrolyte, the resulting ηtotal shows a gradual increase at the beginning of the discharge and peaks at ∼25% depth of discharge (DOD) when Li2S/Li2S2 starts to nucleate (Figures 3g and S16a).
It then slowly decreases before displaying a rapid increase toward the end of the discharge. ηtotal was further decoupled into the three components discussed above (Figure S16b–d).

The resulting ηohm for the MSE-MtBE cell is slightly greater than the DOL/DME cell due to their ionic conductivity difference, with both cells exhibiting a peak value at the nucleation point (2.81 mV for MSE-MtBE and 2.10 mV for DOL/DME) when LiPS concentration reaches its maximum.
However, ηohm takes up only a small fraction of ηtotal, showcasing that it is not the major cause of the cell overpotential.
Meanwhile, the main part of ηtotal is comprised of ηact and ηconc.
Both ηact and ηconc display a peak at ∼ 25% DOD, while ηconc has a rapid increase at the end of the discharge due to more sluggish ion diffusion in the electrode.

The MSE-MtBE cell shows a greater ηact at the Li2S/Li2S2 nucleation point (19.5 mV) compared to the baseline cell (10.4 mV), likely because of reduced LiPS concentration in MSE-MtBE, leading to fewer nuclei and nucleation sites.
The difference is much smaller in ηconc, as it is only slightly larger in MSE-MtBE before 75% DOD.
In fact, the ηconc in MSE- MtBE has a peak value of 44.7 mV at ∼25% DOD, which is lower than that in DOL/DME (47.4 mV).
This is likely due to easier LiPS movement and lower desolvation energy in MSE-MtBE, aligning well with the previous discussion.

Additionally, during termination of discharge, most of the electrochemically active surface is covered; the MSE-MtBE cell shows significantly lower ηconc compared to the baseline cell, thanks to its better wettability and potentially more uniform deposition in the electrode (Figure S17).

Chronoamperometry experiments were further performed to quantitatively study the Li2S nucleation and growth.
As shown in Figure S18, the MSE-MtBE cell achieves a higher response current peak and a larger Li2S deposition capacity of 232 mA h g−1, compared to 161 mA h g−1 for the DOL/DME cell.
This leads to higher discharge capacity and active material utilization in actual Li || S cells.

Interestingly, both chronoamperometry cells show similar peak response time, indicating that MSE-MtBE does not adversely affect the nucleation rate when the polysulfide concentration is the same as in the baseline.
However, in a practical cell with high sulfur loading and low E/S ratio, the nucleation process can also be affected due to polysulfide solubility differences, as discussed in the previous section.
Furthermore, to probe the liquid–liquid sulfur conversion kinetics, temperature-dependent EIS spectra were collected on Li2S6 symmetric cells (Figure S19).
Following a similar procedure applied to Li metal symmetric cells, DRT analysis was carried out to interpret the EIS data (Figures 3h and S20).

DRT peaks appearing at intermediate time constants (10−4 to 10−1 s) are attributed to the Rct of the cell, which is an important indicator of the charge-transfer kinetics.[41,42] These Rct values measured between 0 and 50 °C fit well in an Arrhenius plot, from which activation energies were extracted (Figure 3i).
Interestingly, the MSE-MtBE cell exhibits higher Rct throughout the temperature range, but a lower activation energy compared to DOL/DME.

This suggests that the energy barrier for the charge-transfer process, which is likely associated with desolvation at the electrochemically active surface, is lower in MSE-MtBE, whereas the overall reaction rate is slower, plausibly due to the lower conductivity of MSE-MtBE (Figure S21).

Additionally, in the CV curves of Li2S6 symmetric cells, MSE-MtBE shows slightly lower, but more reversible response current, suggesting fewer side reactions and better stability of the conversion process (Figure S22).

Operando XRD was performed to further elucidate the impact of electrolyte on cathode kinetics and microstructures (Figure 4a,b).
By directly observing the evolution of cathode species, it provides insights into the sulfur conversion process.
Before cycling, both the DOL/DME and MSE-MtBE cells exhibit strong α-S8 signals as expected.
These α-S8 peaks quickly decrease and disappear upon discharge when high and low order LiPSs start to form.
These LiPSs are subsequently converted to low crystallinity Li2S at the end of the discharge, as evidenced by a broad peak detected at around 27°.

Both cells show a complete disappearance of sulfur peaks during discharge, indicating a complete conversion of sulfur, attributed to the optimized spray-dried sulfur composite particles utilized in the cathode.[43] Interestingly, notable differences between the baseline and MSE-MtBE cells were observed after the subsequent charge.

For the DOL/DME cell, a group of β-S8 peaks were detected after charge, which aligns well with previous work in the literature utilizing ether-based electrolytes.[44] However, in the MSE-MtBE cell, β-S8 was first formed toward the end of the charge before peaks corresponding to α-S8 appeared.

Note that α-S8 tends to form when the reaction kinetics move toward solid-state conversion.[32,45] This two-step sulfur deposition process could be characteristic in the MSE due to lower LiPS solubility and regulated solvation properties.
As a kinetically more favorable process, β-S8 is first nucleated from solvated LiPSs, while thermodynamically more stable α-S8 starts to grow when quasi-solid-state reaction kicks in.
Additional ex situ XRD results show that this β – α conversion can happen even on immersing the S cathode retrieved from the DOL/DME cell in MSE-MtBE (Figure S23).

This indicates that MSE- MtBE affects the balance between high order polysulfides and elemental sulfur (in both solution and solid state), thereby changing the dissolution and redeposition process that stabilizes β-S8.
This mechanism may be pivotal toward maintaining adequate charging kinetics, while minimizing LiPS dissolution in MSEs.

Electrochemical Performance of the Electrolytes To evaluate the influence of these altered solvation structures and conversion kinetics on the electrochemical performance, Li || S cells with different electrolytes were assembled and tested under different conditions.
MSE-MtBE and DOL/DME baseline electrolytes were first compared in cells with a relatively low S loading of 2.2 mg cm−2.
Cycled at a rate of C/3 (1C = 1500 mA h g−1), the MSE-MtBE cell exhibits a high initial capacity of 945 mA h g−1 and enables a high retention of 75.2% at 711 mA h g−1 after 200 cycles (Figure S24).
In contrast, DOL/DME only achieves 537 mA h g−1 after 200 cycles, corresponding to a retention of 59.3%.
The increased capacity and capacity retention may benefit from reduced polysulfide dissolution and regulated solvation.
The electrolytes were then demonstrated with a higher S loading of 3.5–3.7 mg cm−2 and a lower E/S ratio of 10 μL mg s−1.

The MSE-MtBE cell maintains a capacity of 710 mA h g−1 after 180 cycles at a C/5 rate, corresponding to 79.4% of its initial capacity, contrasting only 458 mA h g−1 and 56.6% for the DOL/DME cell (Figure 5a, Table S2).
When cycled at a C/10 rate, the MSE-MtBE cell also presents a high initial capacity of 1,019 mA h g−1 and a capacity retention of 83.2% at 848 mA h g−1 after 140 cycles (Figure S25).
The rate performances of the electrolytes were further assessed.
MSE-MtBE achieves higher and more stable capacities at all applied rates (from C/10 to C/2), especially at C/2, where it retains a capacity of 781 mA h g−1 (Figure 5b).
In contrast, the DOL/DME cell only shows a capacity of 700 mA h g−1 and drops below 550 mA h g−1 after 10 cycles at C/2.
Notably, the gap remains significant after the rate changes back to C/5, as the MSE-MtBE cell recovers a capacity of ∼ 850 mA h g−1, while the baseline cell has less than 700 mA h g−1 retained.
Additionally, MSE-MtBE shows comparable overpotentials in the voltage profiles except a larger dip at the nucleation point for the rate of C/2 (Figures 5c and S26).
These results reveal that the addition of MtBE plays an important role in improving the capacity and cyclability of Li– S cells, which may be attributed to its influence on both the electrodes.
Li–S cells with high sulfur loading were further evaluated at an elevated temperature of 45 °C.
Such conditions facilitate the generation and migration of LiPS, while also intensifying detrimental side reactions with Li metal.
With a sulfur loading of 3.6 mg cm−2, the DOL/DME baseline cell shows an initial capacity of 770 mA h g−1 at a C/5 rate and retains 627 mA h g−1 after 90 cycles (Figure 5d).

Even at C/5, the CE rapidly decreases after 30 cycles and averages only 89.4% over the 90 cycles with the baseline electrolyte (Figure S27).

Furthermore, pouch cells were assembled to showcase the performance of MSE-MtBE under more practical conditions.

Surface and Interphase Characterization Interphasial properties play a crucial role in affecting the performance of batteries.
To elucidate the influence of MSE-MtBE on electrode-electrolyte interphases, several characterization tests were carried out.
After cycling the Li || S cells for 30 cycles, Li metal morphology was examined with scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
MSE-MtBE enables dense and uniform Li deposition, packed with large grains, suggesting less parasitic side reactions and dendrite formation (Figure S29).
In contrast, Li metal cycled in DOL/DME has more cracks and non-uniform surface morphology.
The interphasial stability of Li-metal anode is heavily influenced by the characteristics of the SEI layer.
In Li–S systems, SEI forms through the decomposition of electrolyte salt and solvent, as well as the crossover of sulfur-containing species from the cathode.
The modulation of solvation structures and LiPS behaviors by MSE-MtBE may affect the SEI composition.
To better study the SEI in different electrolytes, Li anodes after 30 cycles were evaluated with xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).

As shown in Figure 6a, the S 2p spectra reveal various sulfur species on the surface of the SEI, including SO42−/─SO2 (S 2p3/2 ≈168.7 eV), SO32−/─SO (S 2p3/2 ≈167.1 eV), SB0 (S 2p3/2 ≈163.6 eV), ST−1 (S 2p3/2 ≈161.6 eV), and S−2 (S 2p3/2 ≈159.9 eV).[46] The oxidized sulfur species (─SOx) mainly originate from the LiNO3-involved decomposition of LiTFSI salt and oxidation of soluble LiPSs, while the reduced sulfur species (Sx, x < 0) mainly come from the migration of LiPSs from the cathode.
The MSE-MtBE sample showcases a healthy combination of these species with more oxidized sulfur species detected, which passivate the interphase and promote more reversible Li deposition.
In addition, these oxidized species show slightly lower binding energies compared to the control sample, potentially improving the conductivity of this passivating layer.
On the other hand, the DOL/DME electrolyte leads to the formation of more reduced sulfur species, indicating a greater degree of LiPS shuttling to the anode.
This trend remains unchanged after Ar-cluster ion Angew.

The DOL/DME sample displays significantly stronger signals from reduced sulfur species, which is related to severe LiPS shuttling during the earlier stages of cycling.
Moreover, an inorganic-derived, fluorine-rich SEI is known to improve Li stability.

As shown in the F 1s spectra, both the samples generate C-F (≈688.7 eV) and Li-F (≈ 684.7 eV) species from LiTFSI and solvent decomposition, corresponding to organic and inorganic products, respectively (Figure 6b).
However, the Li anode cycled in MSE-MtBE displays a greater ratio of Li─F to C─F species, demonstrating favorable LiF-enriched compositions in the SEI.

Upon depth profiling with Ar-cluster sputtering, although both samples show increasing intensities of Li─F species as the SEI becomes more inorganic inside, the MSE-MtBE sample maintains a higher concentration of Li─F species compared to DOL/DME (Figure 6c).
This confirms the formation of a more stable SEI with MSE-MtBE, which in turn enhances the stability of Li-metal anode.
XPS was also conducted on the cycled S cathodes in the charged state to probe their surface compositions.

The S cathode cycled in DOL/DME showcases significantly larger amounts of reduced S species (SB0 and ST−1), corresponding to the inactive material resulting from extensive LiPS generation (Figure 6d).[32,47] By contrast, the MSE-MtBE-derived cathode retains a much higher fraction of elemental sulfur (S0, S 2p3/2 ≈164.5 eV) in the charged state.
This can be attributed to the mitigated LiPS shuttling and more complete sulfur conversion, agreeing well with the operando XRD results discussed earlier.

Additionally, stronger peaks of oxidized sulfur species (─SOx) were detected on the DOL/DME-derived cathode, which may originate from unwanted decomposition of electrolyte components and their reactions with sulfur species.
They could also arise from anode-cathode crosstalk owing to the stronger solvating power of the baseline electrolyte.
Unlike the case at the anode, these oxidized sulfur species have less benefits at the cathode surface, but leading to more sluggish ion diffusion.
Finally, the F 1s spectra show a higher Li─F/C─F ratio for the MSE-MtBE cathode, confirming a more inorganic-rich and conductive surface layer (Figure 6e).
Conclusion In summary, we demonstrated an MSE strategy utilizing a family of low-density, low-viscosity, nonfluorinated ether cosolvents that present weaker solvation power than DME.
By probing their intermolecular interactions with salt and solvent, we showed that these co-solvents, especially MtBE, concurrently tune Li+ and polysulfide solvation.

The optimized formulation (MSE-MtBE) effectively (i) weakens Li+– solvent pairing, while increasing Li+–anion association, and (ii) reduces polysulfide dissolution, while improving electrode wettability and mass transport.
As a result, this electrolyte facilitates Li+ desolvation and promotes the formation of a LiF-rich, passivating SEI.
Moreover, these changes produce an altered sulfur deposition pathway that preserves charging Angew.

Manthiram Materials Science and Engineering Program and Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78712, USA E-mail: rmanth@mail.utexas.edu Experimental Section Electrodes Preparation: Ketjenblack (KB, EC-600JD) was first spray-dried following the reported procedure to make the carbon host.[1] Sulfur (75 wt%, ~ 100 mesh, Thermo Scientific) were ground with the spray-dried KB (25 wt%) and melt-diffused in an autoclave at 155 °C for 12 h to obtain the S/KB composite.
The particle sizes of S/KB were further refined with a 45 μm sieve to remove any agglomeration.

To prepare sulfur cathodes, a slurry was produced by mixing the S/KB composite (85 wt%) with carbon nanotube (CNT, 5 wt%, XFNANO), super C65 (5 wt%), polyacrylic acid (PAA, 4 wt%, average MW ≈ 450,000, Sigma-Aldrich), and sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (Na-CMC, 1 wt%, MAC-350) in water in a Thinky mixer.
The slurry was then doctor-blade cast onto carbon-coated aluminum foil and dried at 50 °C under vacuum.
The electrodes were punched into 7/16-in. diameter disks before use.
For pouch cell cathode with a loading of ≥ 4.5 mg cm−2, S/KB composite with 70 wt% sulfur was prepared and mixed with super C 65 (5 wt%) and Na-CMC (4 wt%, MAC-800) in water to obtain the slurry.
Electrolyte Preparation: All electrolytes were prepared in an Ar-filled glovebox.
Solvents were dried with molecular sieves before use.

The baseline electrolyte was composed of 1 M lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI, Solvionic) and 0.2 M LiNO3 (Sigma-Aldrich) in 1,3-dioxolane (DOL, Thermo Scientific) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, Oakwood Chemical) (v/v = 1: 1).
Moderately solvating electrolytes (MSEs) were prepared by dissolving 1 M LiTFSI and 0.2 M LiNO3 in a mixture of DOL, DME, and a moderately solvating solvent (v/v/v = 3.5: 3.5: 3).

The moderately solvating solvents tested include methyl tert-butyl ether (MtBE, Thermo Scientific), cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME, Thermo Scientific), sec-butyl methyl ether (SBME, Sigma-Aldrich), and tert-amyl methyl ether (TAME, Sigma-Aldrich). 0.1 M Li2S6 was added to the electrolytes for assembling Li2S6 symmetric cells.
Electrochemical Measurements: All coin cells were assembled with CR2032 cell cases inside an Ar-filled glovebox.
One layer of Celgard 2325 separator was utilized in each cell.
The electrolyte-to-sulfur (E/S) ratio was controlled (as specified). 20 μL of the electrolyte was added on each side for symmetric cells.
The cells were rested for 5 h before being cycled.
Low loading Li || S cells (~ 2 mg cm−2) were activated with one C/20 cycle and one C/10 cycle.
High loading cells (≥ 3.5 mg cm−2) were first discharged at a C/30 rate, followed by one C/20 formation cycles.
Extra C/10 formation cycles were performed for cells running the C/5 test.
Galvanostatic cycling tests were then performed at specified rates between 1.7 and 2.8 V at 21 °C.
High-temperature cycling test was performed at 45 °C with two C/20 and two C/10 rate formation cycles.
All the cycling data were collected on a Landt or an Arbin cycler.
Galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT) tests were performed at a C/10 rate.
A constant discharge current was applied for 15 min, followed by a 75 min relaxation.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was employed during the rest step (3 min after discharge).
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests were conducted in the potential range of 1.7 to 2.8 V for Li || S cells and −1 to 1 V for Li2S6 symmetric cells.
EIS measurements were conducted in the frequency range of 1 MHz to 0.05 Hz.
Distribution of relaxation time (DRT) analysis was performed with the pyDRTtools package.[2] GITT, CV, and EIS data were collected on a Biologic VMP-3 system.
Pouch Cell Assembly and Testing: Li-S pouch cells were fabricated with Li foil anode and blade-cast sulfur cathode.
The Li anode was pressed onto a Ni current collector.
The cathode was punched into 5.6 × 4.3 cm (~ 24 cm2) sheet, while the anode had a slightly larger dimension (5.8 × 4.5 cm).
Ni and Al tabs were welded onto the anode and cathode current collector, respectively.
The E/S ratio was controlled to be 5.5 or 4.5 μL mg−1.
The pouch cells were put in pressure holders to ensure uniform pressure.
The cells with a sulfur loading of 3.5 mg cm−2 were cycled between 1.7 and 2.8 V at a C/20 rate for 2 formation cycles, followed by cycling at a C/10 rate.
The cells with a loading of 4.6 mg cm−2 were discharged once at a C/30 rate before cycling at a C/20 rate.
Materials Characterization: 1H, 7Li, and 19F nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy was carried out with a Bruker Avance III 500 MHz NMR spectrometer or an Agilent MR400 spectrometer.
Two-dimensional (2D) diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (DOSY) spectra were collected on a Varian 600 MHz NMR spectrometer.
A coaxial insert with 0.1 M LiPF6 dissolved in the deuterated dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO-d6) was applied as the reference.
Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) was performed with a Xenocs Ganesha instrument.
Operando XRD analysis was carried out on a Rigaku Ultima IV X-ray diffractometer with a specially designed cell (MTI Corp).
Raman spectra were collected with a Renishaw Raman spectrometer.
Ionic conductivity of electrolyte was measured with a Mettler-Toledo SevenCompact S230 conductivity meter and an InLab 752 probe.
The surface morphology of the materials was imaged with an Apreo 2C LoVac SEM.
A PHI VersaProbe 4 X-ray Photoelectron Spectrometer was utilized for XPS analysis.
The cycled Li samples were sputtered for various amounts of time with Ar cluster ions.
Computational methods: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations of binding energies were performed with the Gaussian 16 software package.

B3LYP functional and the 6-311+G(d, p) basis set were used for structure optimization of solvent molecules and complexes.[3, 4] Vibrational frequency calculations were conducted to confirm that a local minimum was reached.

M06-2X functional and the ma-def2-TZVP(-f) basis set were used for single point energy calculations.[5, 6] DFT-D3(BJ) and DFT-D3 correction were applied, respectively, for B3LYP and M06-2X to correct the vdW-dispersion energy.[7] The integral equation formalism variant of the polarizable continuum model (IEFPCM) was applied to describe the solvent effect.

The electrostatic potential (ESP) of the solvent molecule was visualized by Multiwfn and Visual Molecular Dynamics (VMD) 1.9.3.[8-10] The binding energy between a solvent molecule and DME or Li+ ion was calculated by the following equation: Classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the electrolytes were performed with the GROMACS 2024 software package.

OPLS-AA force field was chosen for the simulations and Auxiliary Tools of Force Field (AuToFF) tool was applied to parametrize all atoms. 1.2*CM5 charge model was applied to the solvent molecules, while parameters from 0.8*OPLS-2009IL force field were derived for TFSI− and NO3−.[11, 12] The initial coordinates of the molecules were generated by the Packmol program in a 6.5 × 6.5 × 6.5 nm3 simulation box.[13] The numbers of molecules in each simulation cell are listed in Table S3.

The simulation process consists of an initial energy minimization at 0 K with the conjugate gradient method, an initial heating process to 298 K for 1 ns, and a 15 ns run in the NPT ensemble (at 1 bar).
Last 5 ns of the NPT simulation data was used for statistical analysis.
A timestep of 1 fs was used in the simulations.
The C-rescale barostat and V-rescale thermostat were used to control the pressure and temperature, respectively.
Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations for electrolytes with polysulfide were conducted with Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) 6.4.2.

Exchange-correlation potentials were parameterized with the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) employing the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional.[14] The projector augmented wave (PAW) method was used to represent the core electrons and a plane-wave energy cutoff of 550 eV was chosen.[15] The k-point sampling was performed at Gamma point only because of the high computational demands.
The number of molecules in the simulation box was determined based on the electrolyte density.
The initial coordinates of the molecules were generated by the Packmol program.

For MSE-MtBE, 15 DOL, 10 DME, 7 MtBE, 3 LiTFSI, 1 LiNO3, and 1 Li2S6 were placed in a 1.8 × 1.8 × 1.8 nm3 simulation box; for DOL/DME, 20 DOL, 14 DME, 3 LiTFSI, 1 LiNO3, and 1 Li2S6 were placed in a 1.75 × 1.75 × 1.75 nm3 box.
AIMD simulations were conducted at 300 K in the NVT ensemble for 15 ps with last 5 ps of data extracted for statistical analysis.
Temperature was controlled by a Nosé−Hoover thermostat.
Tritium masses on solvents were substituted for protons to allow a timestep of 1 fs.
